content: Many treatments for the common cold are available over-the-counter, but the evidence supporting the effectiveness and safety of nasal decongestants remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and both shortand long-term safety of nasal decongestants used as monotherapy for alleviating symptoms of the common cold in adults and children. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, Web of Science, and clinical trial registries, up to July 2016. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs that compared nasal decongestants to placebo for treating the common cold in adults and children. Quasi-RCTs were excluded. Data were independently extracted by three reviewers, focusing on subjective nasal congestion scores, overall well-being, objective nasal airway resistance, adverse effects, and general recovery. Disagreements were resolved by a fourth reviewer. Trials were categorized into single-dose and multi-dose studies, and oral and topical decongestants were analyzed separately and together. Fifteen trials involving 1838 participants were included. Fourteen studies involved adults aged 18 years or older. Six studies evaluated single-dose interventions, while nine assessed multiple doses. Nine studies used pseudoephedrine, three used oxymetazoline, and others used phenylpropanolamine, norephedrine, or xylometazoline. However, phenylpropanolamine and norephedrine are no longer available on the market, so their results were excluded from meta-analyses. Eleven studies used oral decongestants, and four used topical decongestants. Participants were enrolled after contracting the common cold, with symptom durations varying across studies. In 10 studies, symptoms were present for less than three days; in three studies, symptoms lasted less than five days. One study tracked colds over a year, and another experimentally induced the common cold. Single-dose studies measured effectiveness on the same day, while multi-dose studies followed participants for one to 10 days. Most studies were conducted in university settings, with six at a specific university common cold center. Three studies were conducted in collaboration with hospitals, two in hospital-only settings, and two in unclear settings. Reporting of outcomes and methods was inconsistent, leading to a judgment of low or unclear risk of bias for most studies. Pooling of data was limited due to variability in outcome reporting. Effect sizes were expressed as standardized mean differences (SMDs), with positive SMDs indicating improvement in congestion. SMDs were categorized as small (0.2 to 0.49), moderate (0.5 to 0.79), or large (≥ 0.8). For single-dose decongestants versus placebo, 10 studies compared a single dose of nasal decongestant with placebo, with effectiveness assessed between 15 minutes and 10 hours after dosing. Seven studies reported subjective nasal congestion scores, but none reported overall well-being. Pooling of data was not possible due to variability in symptom measurement and reporting. Two studies reported adverse events, both using oral decongestants, and found no statistical difference in adverse event rates between treatment and placebo groups. For multi-dose decongestants versus placebo, nine studies compared multiple doses of nasal decongestants with placebo, but only five reported subjective nasal congestion scores. Only one study used a topical decongestant, and none reported overall well-being. Subjective congestion scores were significantly better in the treatment group compared to placebo approximately three hours after the last dose (SMD 0.49, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.92; P = 0.02; low-quality evidence). However, the SMD of 0.49 represents only a small clinical effect. Pooling was based on two studies (one oral and one topical), so separate effects of oral and topical decongestants could not be assessed. Seven studies reported adverse events (six oral and one topical decongestant). Meta-analysis showed no statistical difference in adverse event rates between the treatment group (125 per 1000) and the placebo group (126 per 1000). The odds ratio (OR) for adverse events in the treatment group was 0.98 (95% CI 0.68 to 1.40; P = 0.90; low-quality evidence). Results were similar when only oral decongestants were considered (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.39; P = 0.80; low-quality evidence). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of single-dose nasal decongestants. For multiple doses, current evidence suggests a small positive effect on subjective nasal congestion in adults with the common cold, but the clinical relevance of this effect is unclear. There is insufficient high-quality evidence to draw firm conclusions. Due to the limited number of studies using topical decongestants, no conclusions could be drawn about the relative effectiveness of oral versus topical decongestants. Nasal decongestants do not appear to increase the risk of short-term adverse events in adults. The effectiveness and safety of nasal decongestants in children, as well as the clinical significance of their small effect in adults, remain undetermined.
